client: I've been really struggling to focus on my schoolwork since my grandma passed away last month. It's like my brain just shuts down whenever I try to study, and then I start crying when I think about how she'll never get to see me graduate. I'm not sure how talking about it will help when what I really need is to just get back to being productive.
therapist:
It sounds like you're carrying both grief and frustration right now—missing your grandma deeply while also feeling stuck in your schoolwork. When you think about her not being there for graduation, what thoughts or memories come up that feel especially painful? 

Many people find that making space for grief actually helps productivity in the long run—would you be open to exploring how to honor your feelings while gradually rebuilding focus?

client:
I know you're probably right about making space for grief, but it feels impossible to do that without completely falling apart. Whenever I think about graduation, I just remember how excited she was when I got accepted to college - she kept telling all her friends at church about it. Now the thought of walking across that stage without her in the audience makes me feel sick to my stomach. 

And I don't know how to "honor" my feelings when I have three papers due next week. It seems like I have to choose between grieving and functioning, and right now functioning has to win.
therapist:
It sounds like you're caught between two important needs—honoring your love for your grandma and meeting your academic responsibilities. That tension between wanting to grieve fully and needing to function is completely understandable. When those painful thoughts about graduation come up, what's the most difficult part—is it imagining the moment itself without her there, or something deeper about what her presence represented for you?  

Perhaps we could look for small ways to acknowledge your grief that wouldn't overwhelm your schoolwork—have you noticed any moments when remembering her actually brings comfort rather than pain?

client:
It's both, really. The thought of crossing that stage without her cheering me on makes my chest physically ache. But it's also this deeper fear that I didn't appreciate her enough while she was here. I keep remembering times I was too busy with school to visit.  

The happy memories do bring some comfort, but then I feel guilty for feeling okay, like I'm moving on too fast. It's confusing - part of me wants to just cry for days, but I have finals coming up and I can't afford to fall apart.
therapist:
What you're describing—this back-and-forth between comfort and guilt—is actually a very normal part of grieving someone deeply loved. It seems like your mind keeps pulling you between two extremes: either complete emotional shutdown or overwhelming grief. 

I wonder if we could explore this thought that appreciating happy memories means you're "moving on too fast"? Where do you think that belief comes from—has anyone ever implied there's a right timeline for grief, or is this pressure coming from yourself?  

For your finals: what's one small way you could honor your grandma's belief in you while still protecting your study time?

client:
I think the pressure is mostly coming from myself. My family keeps telling me to "be strong" and focus on school, but then I feel guilty when I actually do that. It's like if I'm not constantly sad, I'm betraying her memory somehow. 

That homework feels impossible right now. Every time I try to study, I just think about how she'll never see me graduate, and then I can't concentrate at all. Maybe I'm not ready to honor her belief in me yet—it just makes the loss feel sharper.
therapist:
It sounds like you're caught in a painful cycle—your family's encouragement to "be strong" clashes with your own belief that grief requires constant sadness to prove your love. That inner conflict must feel exhausting on top of your school pressure.  

When you notice that thought about betraying her memory by not being sad, could we examine what your grandma would actually say about that? You knew her best—does that standard of constant grief align with how she lived or what she wanted for you?  

The studying struggle makes complete sense—your mind is trying to process a profound loss. Would it help to experiment with dedicating specific short times for grief (even just 5 minutes) before study sessions, so your feelings have some space without overwhelming your work?

client:
I don't know... Grandma was always telling me to "stop moping" even when she was sick. But now that she's gone, it feels wrong to take her advice. Like if I'm not sad, it means I didn't care enough.  

The timed grief thing sounds scary. What if I start crying and can't stop after 5 minutes? Last time that happened I missed an exam review session and my professor got mad at me.
therapist:
It sounds like you're wrestling with two of your grandma's messages—her practical "stop moping" side and your current fear that easing up on grief means loving her less. That contradiction must feel so confusing.  

What if we reframe those 5 minutes not as a countdown to suppress feelings, but as practice in trusting that grief will still be there later when you need to return to it? Like putting a bookmark in a heavy book—you're not abandoning the story, just pacing yourself.  

When you imagine trying this, what's the smallest step that wouldn't feel overwhelming—maybe just setting a timer to look at one photo of her before studying?

client:
I get what you're saying about the bookmark metaphor, but it still feels like I'm betraying her if I don't stay in the grief. Like if I can function normally, maybe I didn't love her enough. Setting a timer sounds so... clinical? Like I'm scheduling my grief like a dentist appointment. 

The photo idea is okay, but what if looking at her picture just makes me spiral instead of helping me focus? Last time I tried that, I ended up crying for hours and missed my exam anyway.
therapist:
I hear how deeply this belief about grief equaling love is weighing on you—it makes complete sense that scheduling moments to remember her would feel wrong when your heart says the pain should be constant. That loyalty to your grandma's memory is so clear, even in your struggle.  

What if we tried shifting the photo ritual slightly? Instead of aiming to "help you focus," could it simply be a moment to whisper one thing you wish she knew—good or hard—before putting it aside with permission to feel more later? No pressure about how you "should" react.  

When you imagine doing that, does any particular photo come to mind that captures how she really was—not just the loss, but her spirit too?

client:
I like the idea of whispering something to her—that feels more natural than trying to force focus. But I’m scared if I start, I’ll just spiral into crying for hours like last time. There’s this one photo of her laughing in her garden, but even looking at it now makes my chest ache.  

What if I can’t stop once I start? It feels like opening a door I won’t be able to close.
therapist:
It makes complete sense that this photo—even one of her joyful moments—brings both love and ache right now. That fear of the floodgates opening is very real when grief feels so raw.  

Could we try something different? Instead of looking at the photo first, what if you wrote down just one short sentence to whisper to her—something you could read quickly, then put aside—before even taking the photo out? That way, you're setting the container before facing the image.  

When you think of that garden photo, what's one small thing about it that might feel safe to focus on first—the flowers she grew, the way her hands looked, anything that feels like a gentle entry point?

client: I like the idea of writing something down first—that feels less overwhelming than diving straight into the photo. But I’m scared that even one sentence might trigger a full breakdown. What if I can’t stop crying once I start? Her hands... yeah, I remember how they were always covered in dirt from gardening. That’s a softer memory, but it still hurts so much.
therapist:
It sounds like even these softer memories come with such sharp pain right now—like every thread you pull might unravel more than you’re ready for. That fear of being overwhelmed by grief is completely valid.  

What if we practiced with something even smaller than a sentence? Just one word you’d want her to know today—maybe even a mundane one, like “zinnias” if that was her favorite flower. You could write it lightly in pencil, then immediately shift to a grounding action (like splashing water on your face or naming three objects in the room). How does that micro-approach feel—too small, or possibly manageable?  

Her dirt-covered hands tell me she understood growth requires getting a little messy. Do you think she’d want you to have that same patience with yourself right now?

client:
I don't know... even one word feels too heavy right now. What if I write "zinnias" and then just start crying uncontrollably? I'm scared I won't be able to ground myself afterwards. 

But you're right about the dirt on her hands. She was never afraid of getting messy. I just wish I could borrow some of that courage she had. It's hard when I feel so fragile all the time.
therapist:
It sounds like even these small steps feel like standing at the edge of a cliff right now—that fear of losing control is so present. Let me remind you: grief isn't a test of courage, even though it might feel that way. Your fragility right now isn't weakness—it's the price of how deeply you loved her.  

What if we practiced with something even more contained? You could simply trace the *shape* of the word "zinnias" with your finger on the table—no writing, just movement—while breathing out slowly. Would that feel like enough distance to experiment safely?  

When you think of her never fearing messy hands... is there one tiny way you could let yourself be "messy" today without judgment—maybe leaving one textbook open on your bed, or letting a single tear fall without trying to stop it?

client:
The tracing idea feels weirdly overwhelming, even though it seems simple. I can almost hear my mom saying "Don't waste paper" if I start doodling in the air like that. And the messy thing... I don't know, it feels like if I let one tear fall, the whole dam will break and I'll never stop crying.  

I hate how even small things feel impossible right now. Like I'm failing at grieving "correctly" if that makes sense.
therapist:
It sounds like even these small experiments feel loaded with expectations—from your mom's voice in your head to this pressure to grieve "correctly." That added layer of judging yourself for how you're grieving must make everything feel heavier.  

When you imagine that "dam breaking" fear, what's the worst part about it—is it the intensity of the emotions, or the worry about what might happen afterward (like missing responsibilities)?  

Let me ask this: If your grandma saw you holding all this in so tightly, what do you think she'd tell you about those first few tears? Not the floodgates—just those initial drops.
